abstract: Human-level dexterity remains a central open problem in robotics, yet few simulation frameworks cover the full workflow of dexterous manipulation, from setting up a robot to collecting dexterous demonstrations and evaluating policies. We present DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework for dexterous manipulation built on the Genesis simulator. DexSuite provides 30 tasks and assembles its 10 arms and 12 end-effectors, from parallel-jaw grippers to dexterous hands, into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs. It also ships a standardized environment API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated tactile sensing. Moreover, we define a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs spanning diverse contact complexities and horizons, and release a dataset of 4,700 successful episodes in simulation from human teleoperation, scripted experts, and learned policies. We release DexSuite as open source and hope others will build on it. Videos and datasets are available at https://dexsuiteorg.github.io.

sections.body: The paper argues that dexterous hands need first-class benchmark support, since most simulation benchmarks and large teleoperation datasets focus on parallel-jaw grippers. It presents DexSuite, built on the Genesis simulator, with 30 tasks, a standardized environment API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated tactile sensing. It also defines a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs and releases 4,700 successful episodes. The three study questions are whether hand policies match gripper success on identical tasks, how long-horizon tasks affect hand success, and which finger-level tasks remain hard for imitation learning.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: DexSuite offers a simulation framework, benchmark, and dataset for studying dexterous hands against grippers.

sections.body: The related-work section reviews simulators such as Isaac Lab, ManiSkill3, robosuite, RLBench, RoboCasa, and OmniGibson. It says dexterous-hand and gripper tasks are usually separated, bimanual benchmarks are fragmented, and swapping end-effectors on the same scene is uncommon. Dexterous benchmarks such as DexArt and Dactyl each evaluate a single hand model. Large datasets such as DROID and Open X-Embodiment use parallel-jaw grippers, while hand-centric datasets are tied to specific embodiments. DexSuite is positioned to combine GPU-parallel simulation, tactile sensing, native dexterous and bimanual setups, and embodiment-independent tasks in one stack.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing simulators and datasets rarely compare dexterous hands and grippers on identical tasks.

sections.body: DexSuite is a manipulation layer on top of Genesis, which supplies physics, rendering, and parallel simulation. Its 23 rigid-object tasks cover reaching, lifting, pushing, pick-and-place, stacking, and reorientation. Its 7 articulated-object tasks cover mechanisms such as jars and toaster levers. Robots are composed at runtime from independent arm and end-effector models, with a shared Tool Center Point and workspace-aware sampling so object placement adapts to each arm. Tactile pads simulate the FlexiTac sensor on a 12 by 32 taxel grid at 2 mm spacing. Teleoperation supports SpaceMouse, HTC Vive, Meta Quest, and several hand-tracking devices, and all environments follow the Gymnasium interface.
sections.heading: DexSuite
sections.headline: DexSuite adds modular robot composition, workspace-aware sampling, tactile sensing, and teleoperation on Genesis.

sections.body: The benchmark contains 11 tasks in two tracks. Track 1 has five tasks that run with both a parallel-jaw gripper and the Allegro hand, giving a direct embodiment comparison. Track 2 has six tasks completed only with a dexterous hand, four on the Allegro hand and two on the 22-DoF Sharpa Wave hand. These cover stable grasping, constrained transport, tool use, multi-object interaction, and long-horizon manipulation. The dataset holds 4,700 successful episodes: 700 human teleoperation demonstrations, 1,200 scripted demonstrations, and 2,800 successful policy rollouts. All trajectories share one observation and action format and are released in LeRobot and HDF5 formats.
sections.heading: Benchmark & Dataset
sections.headline: The benchmark pairs 11 tasks in two tracks into 16 task-embodiment pairs, with 4,700 released episodes.

sections.body: Five imitation learning baselines were trained on 50 human demonstrations per task, except the last two long-horizon tasks, which used 200 scripted demonstrations. Each selected checkpoint was re-evaluated on three new seeds with 50 episodes each. The embodiment gap depends on task and policy: BC-T reaches 76% on Pick & Place with the hand versus 64% with the gripper, while ACT, which is action chunking with a transformer, reaches 66% with the gripper versus 60% with the hand. Sequential tasks drop sharply: the best state-based policies reach 16% on Stack with the gripper and 9% with Allegro. The authors note that with 50 episodes the standard error can reach 7 points, so gaps of a few points should be read with care.
sections.heading: Experiments and Results
sections.headline: Baselines reach 89% on Move Pan but at most 16% on Stack, with embodiment effects depending on task and policy.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes DexSuite as a framework built on Genesis, together with a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs and a dataset of 4,700 successful episodes. Policies trained on a dexterous hand match or outperform their gripper counterparts on several shared tasks. Precise tool use and sequential object manipulation remain difficult. The authors release the framework, benchmark, and dataset as open source. Contributors can add new environments as one class on the standard API, and new arms, hands, and sensors without changing task code.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: A hand matches or beats a gripper on several shared tasks, but precise tool use and sequential manipulation stay hard.
